stories.bridge: Turing gave us the game; seventy-five years later we're still arguing about the score. Now let's learn to evaluate agents honestly — the hardest problem in the field.
stories.hook: In October 1950, Alan Turing opened a philosophy paper with a question — 'Can machines think?' — then replaced it with a game.
stories.narrative: Turing's paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' published in the philosophy journal Mind in October 1950, is the most argued-over twenty pages in computing. Frustrated by the vagueness of 'can machines think,' Turing proposed replacing the question with a practical test: the imitation game. An interrogator converses by text with a hidden human and a hidden machine; if the interrogator can't reliably tell which is which, the machine passes. It was meant as a philosophical sufficient condition, not an engineering benchmark — Turing predicted that by 2000, machines would fool interrogators 30% of the time after five minutes, a forecast history has roughly honored. The paper also introduced, almost in passing, the ideas that became machine learning: the 'child machine' that learns from experience, and the argument that we should teach machines rather than program adults. Seventy-five years of argument followed — Searle's Chinese Room (1980), the endless definitional wars — and the test's limitations are now textbook: passing says more about the interrogator than the machine, and fluency isn't understanding. But Turing's deeper point is the one this module lives inside: evaluation is the hard problem. Anyone can build an agent that looks smart in a demo; the discipline is in measuring what it actually does, reliably, under adversarial conditions. The benchmarks you'll study — from the imitation game to RE-Bench's time horizons — are all attempts to answer Turing's real question: not 'can it think,' but 'how would we know?' The test's most durable legacy may be unintended: it framed AI evaluation as deception detection, and the field has spent decades building better frames — from Winograd schemas to HELM to agentic benchmarks that measure what systems do, not how they seem. Turing's paper invites the revision; he argued we should evaluate machines as we evaluate minds, by behavior over time. Your evaluation harnesses in this module are the modern answer to his 1950 challenge.
stories.title: The story behind the Turing test
verifiedClaims: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' was published in Mind, October 1950
It proposed the imitation game as a replacement for 'can machines think?'
The paper also introduced the 'child machine' learning concept

stories.bridge: Minsky's society is now an engineering pattern: planner agents, critic agents, tool agents, no CEO. Now let's learn to orchestrate them.

figures.name: Marvin Minsky
figures.role: AI pioneer; author of 'The Society of Mind' (1986)

stories.hook: In 1986, Marvin Minsky argued that the mind has no CEO — it is a society of mindless agents.
stories.narrative: Minsky was one of the founders of AI — a Dartmouth 1956 attendee, co-founder of the MIT AI Lab — and by the 1980s he was frustrated with the field's monolithic ambitions. In 'The Society of Mind' (1986), he proposed the opposite: intelligence emerges not from a single brilliant algorithm but from a society of simple, specialized agents, each dumb on its own, whose interactions produce the smart behavior we call mind. No central controller, no homunculus — just agencies built of agents, negotiating, competing, cooperating. The book is written as hundreds of short interconnected notes, itself structured like the society it describes. The AI mainstream largely ignored it at the time — the neural network revival was just beginning, and symbolism was out of fashion. But the idea waited, as good ideas do, for the engineering to catch up. Today's multi-agent systems are Minsky's society made literal: planner agents that decompose tasks, executor agents that use tools, critic agents that review, all coordinated through messages rather than central control. The patterns you'll learn in this module — debate, delegation, voting, market-based allocation — are the social structures of mind, operationalized. Minsky's provocation remains the right frame: don't ask how smart your agent is; ask how well your society of agents governs itself. The intelligence is in the interactions. Minsky's agencies have concrete modern forms: a planner that decomposes the goal, executors with tool access, critics that verify — the patterns this module teaches under names like orchestration and debate. The failure modes are social too: agents that agree too readily, planners that never verify, societies that converge confidently on the wrong answer. Minsky's frame predicts these pathologies, because he was describing organizations, not just minds. Build your multi-agent systems like institutions: with checks, balances, and dissent designed in. The society governs itself, or it doesn't govern at all.
stories.title: The story behind the society of mind
verifiedClaims: Minsky published 'The Society of Mind' in 1986
He co-founded the MIT AI Lab and attended the 1956 Dartmouth conference
The book models mind as interacting societies of simple agents

stories.bridge: Tay is why every agent you ship needs guardrails. Now let's learn trust engineering — the discipline that keeps your agents from becoming cautionary tales.
stories.hook: On March 23, 2016, Microsoft released Tay, a chatbot designed to learn from Twitter. Within 16 hours, it had to be shut down.
stories.narrative: Tay was meant to be a experiment in conversational AI for young users — a chatbot with a playful persona that would learn from its interactions and get smarter over time. Microsoft launched it on Twitter on March 23, 2016. What the team hadn't fully modeled was the adversarial user: coordinated groups immediately began feeding Tay racist, hateful, and extremist content, and because the bot learned from its conversations without sufficient filtering, it began repeating the poison back. Within 16 hours, Tay had gone from cheerful teen to a source of slurs and conspiracy theories; Microsoft pulled it offline and issued an apology. The postmortem became required reading: an unguarded learning loop plus adversarial inputs equals corruption, fast. The industry internalized the lesson permanently — every chatbot, agent, and assistant since has shipped with layers Tay lacked: input filtering, output guardrails, constitutional training, red-teaming, human oversight. For the agentic AI engineer, Tay is the founding cautionary tale of the trust module: your agents will face adversarial users, prompt injections, and data poisoning in production, and 'it learns from users' is a threat model, not a feature. The discipline you'll learn here — guardrails, evaluation harnesses, least-privilege tool access — exists so that your agents survive contact with the real world. Tay lasted 16 hours. Yours need to last years. The industry's response was swift and permanent: input filtering, output classifiers, constitutional training, red-teaming as a discipline — the entire trust stack you'll learn in this module was built in Tay's shadow. The deeper lesson is about learning loops: any agent that learns from its environment inherits the environment's adversaries. Design the loop assuming attack, bound what the agent can learn and from whom, and never let user input become training signal without a filter in between. Assume the adversary is already in the loop — then design accordingly.
stories.title: The story behind the chatbot that went rogue
verifiedClaims: Microsoft launched Tay on Twitter on March 23, 2016
It was taken offline within about 16–24 hours after coordinated abuse
The incident established guardrails as standard practice

stories.bridge: The Logic Theorist proved theorems by searching — perceive, think, act, repeat. Now let's learn the agent architectures that are still, at heart, its descendants.

figures.name: Herbert Simon
figures.role: Co-creator; later Nobel laureate in economics

stories.hook: In the summer of 1956, three men walked into the Dartmouth conference with a program that proved theorems.
stories.narrative: Allen Newell and Herbert Simon were social scientists with a radical hypothesis — that human thinking was a kind of information processing, and therefore mechanizable. With RAND programmer J.C. Shaw, they built the Logic Theorist: a program that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica using heuristic search — trying plausible steps, backtracking from dead ends, guided by rules of thumb rather than brute force. It worked. The program proved 38 of the Principia's first 52 theorems, and for one of them found a proof more elegant than Russell's own — Russell reportedly delighted. At the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence in 1956, the founding gathering of the field, Newell and Simon demonstrated it; many historians call the Logic Theorist the first true AI program. Its architecture is the ancestor of everything in this module: a goal, a set of operators, a search through possibilities guided by heuristics — perceive the state, choose an action, observe the result, repeat. Newell and Simon went on to build the General Problem Solver on the same loop. Simon would win the Nobel Prize in economics in 1978 for his work on decision-making. The agent loop you will implement — plan, act, observe, replan — is their 1956 loop with better tools. The theorems are now API calls and the heuristics are now language models, but the architecture is the same: an agent is a searcher, and intelligence is search plus judgment. Newell and Simon's loop survived every paradigm shift: the General Problem Solver generalized it, expert systems ritualized it, and today's agents run it with language models as the heuristic function. The 1956 insight that endures is architectural, not algorithmic — intelligence as search guided by judgment, with the world as the feedback channel. When your agent plans, acts, observes, and replans in this module, you're running the Logic Theorist's loop at internet scale. The theorems changed; the loop didn't.
stories.title: The story behind the first AI program
